headline: The AI boom is becoming a market risk as well as a growth engine
dek: The United States is reassessing huge AI investments, while Japan and South Korea feel the shock through markets and semiconductors. China is managing the currency effects of strong external demand.
story_title: AI’s global economic test: growth, exports, and market nerves
story_html:
United States 🇺🇸 Wall Street’s enthusiasm for artificial intelligence has abruptly become more cautious. On Thursday, November 5, shares linked to AI chips, software, and data-center construction suffered a severe sell-off. The Nasdaq fell toward correction territory, while investors questioned whether the enormous capital spending required for AI infrastructure can generate returns quickly enough. Political uncertainty also mattered: after the midterm elections, investors began to worry that a new Congress could impose tighter limits on data centers or slow the expansion of the electricity network they require. The immediate damage was concentrated in technology stocks, but the episode matters for the wider economy because AI investment has been supporting growth, corporate profits, and demand for skilled workers. At the same time, the labor market still looks relatively resilient: weekly applications for unemployment benefits fell to 189,000, the lowest level since mid-July. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/7ee9c212805aa5e70cf34d25aab7a36e?utm_source=openai))

China 🇨🇳 China’s story is less about a sudden stock-market shock and more about managing the consequences of strong external demand. The People’s Bank of China said it would raise the foreign-exchange reserve requirement ratio from 4% to 6% on November 15. In practical terms, banks will have to hold more foreign currency, reducing the supply of dollars available for conversion into yuan. The move is designed to slow the yuan’s appreciation after robust exports, a large trade surplus, and companies’ conversion of foreign earnings pushed the currency higher. A stronger yuan can reduce the domestic value of exporters’ overseas revenues, even though it makes imported goods and energy cheaper. Beijing therefore appears to be balancing two objectives: preserving export competitiveness while preventing excessive one-way bets on the currency. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/china-to-raise-forex-deposit-reserve-ratio-to-6-starting-november-15-4993312?utm_source=openai))

Japan 🇯🇵 Japan shows how quickly a U.S. technology shock can travel through Asian financial markets. The Nikkei 225 fell more than 6% after trading opened on Friday, November 6, as investors sold companies exposed to semiconductors, automation, and the construction of AI data centers. The yen, meanwhile, remained weak at roughly ¥158 to the dollar, a combination that can support exporters but also raises the cost of imported fuel and food. Corporate results were not uniformly negative: Toyota raised its full-year profit forecast even though quarterly profit declined, suggesting that established manufacturers can still benefit from strong overseas sales and currency effects. Japan’s economy is therefore caught between two forces—an export sector that can profit from a weak yen and a market increasingly sensitive to the sustainability of the AI investment cycle. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/bba6f0bf9035a6e6b1c4fef3e8230b89?utm_source=openai))

South Korea 🇰🇷 South Korea is the clearest example of the AI boom’s real-economy benefits—and its financial vulnerability. October exports jumped 93.7% year on year to a record $115.3 billion, while semiconductor exports soared 259% to $56.4 billion. Demand for memory chips used in AI servers has transformed the trade figures and put the country on course to exceed $1 trillion in annual exports. Yet the same dependence creates risk: when U.S. investors suddenly question data-center spending, Korean chipmakers and the KOSPI can fall sharply even if factory orders remain strong. The common theme across these four economies is not a single shared slowdown. It is a change in the quality of AI-led growth: the technology is still lifting trade and investment, but markets are demanding clearer proof that the spending is economically sustainable. ([en.yna.co.kr](https://en.yna.co.kr/view/AEN20261101000900320?section=economy-finance%2Feconomy&utm_source=openai))
b2_summary: The AI boom is affecting the four economies in different ways. In the United States, investors sold technology shares because they worried that huge data-center investments may be too expensive or face political limits. Japan’s stock market fell as the shock spread across Asia, although Toyota raised its profit forecast. China is trying to slow the yuan’s rise after strong exports increased demand for the currency. South Korea is benefiting strongly from AI-related chip demand: October exports rose almost 94%. The shared theme is that AI still supports growth, but investors now want stronger evidence that the boom can continue.

concept.title: Why can a stronger currency hurt exporters?
concept.explanation: When a country’s currency rises, its companies receive fewer units of local currency when they convert overseas sales back home. This can reduce reported profits and make their products more expensive for foreign buyers. However, imports such as oil, machinery, and food become cheaper. The overall effect depends on how important exports and imports are to the economy.

quiz.question: Why is South Korea especially sensitive to a slowdown in AI data-center investment?
options: Because it imports almost all of its food from the United States
Because semiconductors make up a large and rapidly growing share of its exports
Because the Bank of Korea controls the yuan’s exchange rate
quiz.explanation: South Korea’s export surge is being powered by semiconductor demand, especially for AI servers. A slowdown in data-center construction could therefore reduce orders for Korean chipmakers.

one_sentence: The AI boom is still generating growth, but the world is moving from asking “How fast can it expand?” to “Can the spending pay off?”
